PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child &#38 Family Services Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers-teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 1 WAS SUBMITTED.

## AUTHORIZES $6.38 BILLION IN BONDS TO BUILD MENTAL HEALTH TREATMENT FACILITIES FOR THOSE WITH MENTAL HEALTH AND SUBSTANCE USE CHALLENGES; PROVIDES HOUSING FOR THE HOMELESS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
### OVERVIEW
Proposition 1 has two major components related to providing mental health care and drug or alcohol treatment to people and addressing homelessness.
The proposition:
- Changes the Mental Health Services Act that was passed by voters in 2004, with a focus on how the money from the act can be used.
- Approves a $6.4 billion bond to build (1) more places for mental health care and drug or alcohol treatment and (2) more housing for people with mental health, drug, or alcohol challenges.
### MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES ACT
#### PROPOSAL
***State Gets Larger Share of Tax.*** As shown in Figure 1, Proposition 1 increases the share of the MHSA tax that the state gets for mental health programs.
The proposition also requires the state to spend a dedicated amount of its MHSA money on increasing the number of mental health care workers and preventing mental illness and drug or alcohol addiction across communities.
Because the state would receive a larger share of the tax, counties would receive a somewhat smaller share.
***Changes to How Counties Provide Services.*** Proposition 1 requires that counties spend more of their MHSA money on housing and personalized support services like employment assistance and education.

...
### SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
- Shift roughly $140 million annually of existing tax revenue for mental health, drug, and alcohol treatment from counties to the state.
- Increased state costs to repay bonds of about $310 million annually for 30 years.
These bond funds would be used to build (1) more places where people can get mental health care and drug or alcohol treatment and (2) more housing for people with mental health, drug, or alcohol challenges.

# Proposition Guide
## BEHAVIORAL HEALTH SERVICES PROGRAM AND BOND MEASURE.
CAIR-CA holds reservations regarding Proposition 1’s potential impact on (1) involuntary treatment centers and communities of color, (2) reallocation of county funds, and (3) narrowing of MHSA recipients.
(1) California has made large strides in reducing investments into involuntary/forced/locked treatment options for persons with severe behavioral needs.
These types of facilities are not trauma-informed, evidence-backed, and disproportionately admit people of color.
By reinvesting in housing interventions which include these forms of treatment, California risks regressing into discriminatory and ineffective systems of care.
(2) County funds currently finance community-based services and supports.
Proposition 1 would reallocate these funds to housing interventions with an additional percentage reallocated to the state budget, thus decentering local, community-based resources.
(3) The Mental Health Services Act currently serves a spectrum of behavioral health needs and Proposition 1 would shift funding towards a subset of the population with the most severe needs, thus affecting intervention and prevention services provided by the counties.

Proposition 1 would issue $6.38 billion in bonds to build supportive housing and residential treatment facilities.
It would also amend the Mental Health Services
Act (a 1% tax on personal income over $1 million), allowing funds to also be used to help residents with substance abuse, not just those with mental illness.
And it would set aside 30% of revenue generated from that tax to help house people
—!particularly veterans — with behavioral health conditions.!
Yes Argument
California should focus its resources on supporting residents who have severe mental health and substance abuse issues and keep them from living on the streets.
Proposition 1 will provide a reliable funding source to build treatment facilities and it will dedicate over $1 billion toward supportive housing for veterans with behavioral health challenges.
The current rules of the Mental Health Services Act are too restrictive and should be changed to help people struggling with serious substance abuse issues.
No Argument
Proposition 1 pulls revenue from the Mental Health Services Act in too many new directions.
If you are increasing the amount of MHSA money going toward housing and residents with substance abuse issues, there will be less left for existing mental health services.
Additionally, the bond money can be used to build locked facilities, which are a threat to civil liberties and will take California back to the era of involuntary treatment for severe mental illness.!

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child &#38 Family Services Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers-teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 1 WAS SUBMITTED.

## AUTHORIZES $6.38 BILLION IN BONDS TO BUILD MENTAL HEALTH TREATMENT FACILITIES FOR THOSE WITH MENTAL HEALTH AND SUBSTANCE USE CHALLENGES; PROVIDES HOUSING FOR THE HOMELESS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
### OVERVIEW
Proposition 1 has two major components related to providing mental health care and drug or alcohol treatment to people and addressing homelessness.
The proposition:
- Changes the Mental Health Services Act that was passed by voters in 2004, with a focus on how the money from the act can be used.
- Approves a $6.4 billion bond to build (1) more places for mental health care and drug or alcohol treatment and (2) more housing for people with mental health, drug, or alcohol challenges.
### MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES ACT
#### PROPOSAL
***State Gets Larger Share of Tax.*** As shown in Figure 1, Proposition 1 increases the share of the MHSA tax that the state gets for mental health programs.
The proposition also requires the state to spend a dedicated amount of its MHSA money on increasing the number of mental health care workers and preventing mental illness and drug or alcohol addiction across communities.
Because the state would receive a larger share of the tax, counties would receive a somewhat smaller share.
***Changes to How Counties Provide Services.*** Proposition 1 requires that counties spend more of their MHSA money on housing and personalized support services like employment assistance and education.

Proposition 1 would issue $6.38 billion in bonds to build supportive housing and residential treatment facilities.

Yes Argument
California should focus its resources on supporting residents who have severe mental health and substance abuse issues and keep them from living on the streets.
Proposition 1 will provide a reliable funding source to build treatment facilities and it will dedicate over $1 billion toward supportive housing for veterans with behavioral health challenges.

No Argument
Proposition 1 pulls revenue from the Mental Health Services Act in too many new directions.
If you are increasing the amount of MHSA money going toward housing and residents with substance abuse issues, there will be less left for existing mental health services.

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 1
YES ON PROP. 1: AFFORDABLE HOMES FOR VETERANS, SENIORS, PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES AND WORKING FAMILIES-WITHOUT RAISING TAXES
All Californians deserve a safe and affordable place to call home, but California has a housing shortage that is driving the nation’s worst housing affordability crisis. More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.
Prop. 1 gives Californians the opportunity to:
Fast-track housing production;
Provide housing to working families, veterans, people with disabilities and seniors;
Help prevent homelessness by keeping our most vulnerable neighbors in their homes;
Expands homeownership opportunities;
Maintains strict fiscal accountability and transparency with NO NEW TAXES.
PROP. 1 HONORS OUR VETERANS
Dedicates $1.25 billion solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership opportunities through the existing CalVet Home Loan Program, which has already helped almost a million veterans and their families.
“California has one of the largest populations of homeless veterans in the nation. After their service, our veterans deserve a place to call home. Prop. 1 delivers on that promise.”-Michael Blecker, President, CA Association of Veteran Service Agencies
PROP. 1 BUILDS HOMES LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES CAN AFFORD
Prop. 1 jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes across California, quickly turning stalled construction into move-in ready homes. The teacher in your child’s classroom, the firefighter who protects your neighborhood, first-time homebuyers, low- and middle-income Californians, and the nurse at your local hospital can no longer afford to live in most California communities. Prop. 1 builds more homes working people can actually afford.
NO NEW TAXES-STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY
Prop. 1 doesn’t raise taxes and every dollar comes with strict accountability and public reporting. Voters will be able to see exactly how many homes get built, where, and at what cost. Prop. 1 unlocks federal matching funds, bringing tax dollars we send to Washington back home to California.
PROP. 1 HELPS SENIORS, VETERANS & OUR MOST VULNERABLE
Prop. 1 creates and preserves housing to help those who are one crisis away from homelessness stay off the streets, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, veterans, at risk and foster youth, and people with disabilities who all deserve safe and stable homes.
PROP. 1 INVESTS IN COMMUNITIES & ESSENTIAL WORKERS
Quality, affordable housing is the foundation of thriving communities. Prop. 1 strengthens that foundation by helping essential workers-from firefighters and teachers to nurses-afford to live in the communities they serve. Working families and essential workers across California are being priced out and left behind. Prop. 1 enables the construction of affordable housing for these essential workers who dedicate their lives to our communities.
YES ON PROP. 1: SUPPORTED BY VETERANS, SENIORS, TEACHERS, FIREFIGHTERS, AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES including Habitat for Humanity California, California Alliance for Retired Americans, Housing California, California Housing Consortium, California Alliance of Child and Family Services.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 1, Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond, to honor those veterans who served; provide safe and stable housing to California’s most vulnerable; guarantee strict fiscal accountability with no new taxes; and build the affordable homes all Californians deserve.

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including for California veterans, and to finance housing development projects seeking federal tax credits.
Allocates funds:
$5.1 billion to build and rehabilitate multifamily rental housing;
$2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate, or preserve affordable housing units, and provide supportive housing for those experiencing homelessness;
$1.25 billion for state-funded mortgages for California veterans;
$1.1 billion for homeownership and downpayment assistance;
$1 billion for farmworker, tribal, and student housing;
$500 million for housing infrastructure; and
$200 million to support local housing programs.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 1
YES ON PROP. 1: AFFORDABLE HOMES FOR VETERANS, SENIORS, PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES AND WORKING FAMILIES-WITHOUT RAISING TAXES
All Californians deserve a safe and affordable place to call home, but California has a housing shortage that is driving the nation’s worst housing affordability crisis. More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.
Prop. 1 gives Californians the opportunity to:
Fast-track housing production;
Provide housing to working families, veterans, people with disabilities and seniors;
Help prevent homelessness by keeping our most vulnerable neighbors in their homes;
Expands homeownership opportunities;
Maintains strict fiscal accountability and transparency with NO NEW TAXES.
PROP. 1 HONORS OUR VETERANS
Dedicates $1.25 billion solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership opportunities through the existing CalVet Home Loan Program, which has already helped almost a million veterans and their families.
“California has one of the largest populations of homeless veterans in the nation. After their service, our veterans deserve a place to call home. Prop. 1 delivers on that promise.”-Michael Blecker, President, CA Association of Veteran Service Agencies
PROP. 1 BUILDS HOMES LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES CAN AFFORD
Prop. 1 jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes across California, quickly turning stalled construction into move-in ready homes. The teacher in your child’s classroom, the firefighter who protects your neighborhood, first-time homebuyers, low- and middle-income Californians, and the nurse at your local hospital can no longer afford to live in most California communities. Prop. 1 builds more homes working people can actually afford.
NO NEW TAXES-STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY
Prop. 1 doesn’t raise taxes and every dollar comes with strict accountability and public reporting. Voters will be able to see exactly how many homes get built, where, and at what cost. Prop. 1 unlocks federal matching funds, bringing tax dollars we send to Washington back home to California.
PROP. 1 HELPS SENIORS, VETERANS & OUR MOST VULNERABLE
Prop. 1 creates and preserves housing to help those who are one crisis away from homelessness stay off the streets, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, veterans, at risk and foster youth, and people with disabilities who all deserve safe and stable homes.
PROP. 1 INVESTS IN COMMUNITIES & ESSENTIAL WORKERS
Quality, affordable housing is the foundation of thriving communities. Prop. 1 strengthens that foundation by helping essential workers-from firefighters and teachers to nurses-afford to live in the communities they serve. Working families and essential workers across California are being priced out and left behind. Prop. 1 enables the construction of affordable housing for these essential workers who dedicate their lives to our communities.
YES ON PROP. 1: SUPPORTED BY VETERANS, SENIORS, TEACHERS, FIREFIGHTERS, AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES including Habitat for Humanity California, California Alliance for Retired Americans, Housing California, California Housing Consortium, California Alliance of Child and Family Services.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 1, Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond, to honor those veterans who served; provide safe and stable housing to California’s most vulnerable; guarantee strict fiscal accountability with no new taxes; and build the affordable homes all Californians deserve.

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including for California veterans, and to finance housing development projects seeking federal tax credits.
Allocates funds:
$5.1 billion to build and rehabilitate multifamily rental housing;
$2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate, or preserve affordable housing units, and provide supportive housing for those experiencing homelessness;
$1.25 billion for state-funded mortgages for California veterans;
$1.1 billion for homeownership and downpayment assistance;
$1 billion for farmworker, tribal, and student housing;
$500 million for housing infrastructure; and
$200 million to support local housing programs.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 1
YES ON PROP. 1: AFFORDABLE HOMES FOR VETERANS, SENIORS, PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES AND WORKING FAMILIES-WITHOUT RAISING TAXES
All Californians deserve a safe and affordable place to call home, but California has a housing shortage that is driving the nation’s worst housing affordability crisis. More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.
Prop. 1 gives Californians the opportunity to:
Fast-track housing production;
Provide housing to working families, veterans, people with disabilities and seniors;
Help prevent homelessness by keeping our most vulnerable neighbors in their homes;
Expands homeownership opportunities;
Maintains strict fiscal accountability and transparency with NO NEW TAXES.
PROP. 1 HONORS OUR VETERANS
Dedicates $1.25 billion solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership opportunities through the existing CalVet Home Loan Program, which has already helped almost a million veterans and their families.
“California has one of the largest populations of homeless veterans in the nation. After their service, our veterans deserve a place to call home. Prop. 1 delivers on that promise.”-Michael Blecker, President, CA Association of Veteran Service Agencies
PROP. 1 BUILDS HOMES LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES CAN AFFORD
Prop. 1 jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes across California, quickly turning stalled construction into move-in ready homes. The teacher in your child’s classroom, the firefighter who protects your neighborhood, first-time homebuyers, low- and middle-income Californians, and the nurse at your local hospital can no longer afford to live in most California communities. Prop. 1 builds more homes working people can actually afford.
NO NEW TAXES-STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY
Prop. 1 doesn’t raise taxes and every dollar comes with strict accountability and public reporting. Voters will be able to see exactly how many homes get built, where, and at what cost. Prop. 1 unlocks federal matching funds, bringing tax dollars we send to Washington back home to California.
PROP. 1 HELPS SENIORS, VETERANS & OUR MOST VULNERABLE
Prop. 1 creates and preserves housing to help those who are one crisis away from homelessness stay off the streets, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, veterans, at risk and foster youth, and people with disabilities who all deserve safe and stable homes.
PROP. 1 INVESTS IN COMMUNITIES & ESSENTIAL WORKERS
Quality, affordable housing is the foundation of thriving communities. Prop. 1 strengthens that foundation by helping essential workers-from firefighters and teachers to nurses-afford to live in the communities they serve. Working families and essential workers across California are being priced out and left behind. Prop. 1 enables the construction of affordable housing for these essential workers who dedicate their lives to our communities.
YES ON PROP. 1: SUPPORTED BY VETERANS, SENIORS, TEACHERS, FIREFIGHTERS, AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES including Habitat for Humanity California, California Alliance for Retired Americans, Housing California, California Housing Consortium, California Alliance of Child and Family Services.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 1, Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond, to honor those veterans who served; provide safe and stable housing to California’s most vulnerable; guarantee strict fiscal accountability with no new taxes; and build the affordable homes all Californians deserve.

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. California Prop. 1: $11.25B housing bond draws support from developers, concerns over state debt
BY
Anna Albaryan (https://spectrumlocalnews.com/ca/california/reporters/2022/09/29/anna-albaryan)
West Los Angeles
PUBLISHED 1:40 PM PT Oct. 16, 2026
PUBLISHED 1:40 PM PDT Oct. 16, 2026
SHARE
LOS ANGELES — California voters will decide this November whether to authorize $11.25 billion in new state borrowing to address the housing crisis through Proposition 1, a measure supported by housing advocates and developers but criticized by opponents concerned about the state’s growing debt.
In West Los Angeles, housing developers Daniel Glimcher and Simon Aftalian of PASSO (https://www.livepasso.com/) are working to expand affordable housing for veterans near the West LA VA Medical Center.
One of their latest projects, a 53-unit apartment building on Stoner Avenue, is expected to be completed in December.
The developers said they plan to deliver 3,000 apartments for veterans over the next four years.
Glimcher says their developments are designed with veterans’ needs in mind, from calming interior colors to locations near the West Los Angeles Veterans Affairs Medical Center and other resources, including public transportation.
Both developers support Proposition 1, even though their projects would not necessarily receive funding from the measure.
What would Proposition 1 do?
If approved, Proposition 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds, including $10 billion for affordable housing construction, preservation and homeownership assistance. The remaining $1.25 billion would support home loans for veterans.
Supporters argue the investment could help address California’s housing shortage as developers face challenges securing adequate funding.
But opponents, including Republican state Sen. Tony Strickland, who represents Huntington Beach, argue the state cannot afford additional debt.
“These billions of dollars in bonds, what that is, it’s maxing out your credit card at a time when we know the state is going to have a structural budget deficit,” Strickland said.
According to the state’s Legislative Analyst’s Office, repaying the $10 billion housing bond would cost approximately $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years. The veterans’ home loan portion would be repaid through mortgage payments.
For developers like Glimcher and Aftalian, the measure represents another potential investment in addressing California’s housing needs. For critics, the question is whether the long-term benefits justify the cost.
Voters will decide the fate of Proposition 1 in the Nov. 3 general election.

They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. California Prop. 1: $11.25B housing bond draws support from developers, concerns over state debt
BY
Anna Albaryan (https://spectrumlocalnews.com/ca/california/reporters/2022/09/29/anna-albaryan)
West Los Angeles
PUBLISHED 1:40 PM PT Oct. 16, 2026
PUBLISHED 1:40 PM PDT Oct. 16, 2026
SHARE
LOS ANGELES — California voters will decide this November whether to authorize $11.25 billion in new state borrowing to address the housing crisis through Proposition 1, a measure supported by housing advocates and developers but criticized by opponents concerned about the state’s growing debt.
In West Los Angeles, housing developers Daniel Glimcher and Simon Aftalian of PASSO (https://www.livepasso.com/) are working to expand affordable housing for veterans near the West LA VA Medical Center.
One of their latest projects, a 53-unit apartment building on Stoner Avenue, is expected to be completed in December.
The developers said they plan to deliver 3,000 apartments for veterans over the next four years.
Glimcher says their developments are designed with veterans’ needs in mind, from calming interior colors to locations near the West Los Angeles Veterans Affairs Medical Center and other resources, including public transportation.
Both developers support Proposition 1, even though their projects would not necessarily receive funding from the measure.
What would Proposition 1 do?
If approved, Proposition 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds, including $10 billion for affordable housing construction, preservation and homeownership assistance. The remaining $1.25 billion would support home loans for veterans.
Supporters argue the investment could help address California’s housing shortage as developers face challenges securing adequate funding.
But opponents, including Republican state Sen. Tony Strickland, who represents Huntington Beach, argue the state cannot afford additional debt.
“These billions of dollars in bonds, what that is, it’s maxing out your credit card at a time when we know the state is going to have a structural budget deficit,” Strickland said.
According to the state’s Legislative Analyst’s Office, repaying the $10 billion housing bond would cost approximately $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years. The veterans’ home loan portion would be repaid through mortgage payments.
For developers like Glimcher and Aftalian, the measure represents another potential investment in addressing California’s housing needs. For critics, the question is whether the long-term benefits justify the cost.
Voters will decide the fate of Proposition 1 in the Nov. 3 general election.

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students.
